summary: The change stops TypeCollector from indexing empty DeclaringSyntaxReferences for metadata-only symbols, using FirstOrDefault for the property and member-needs-key diagnostics. It also wraps the analyzer diagnostic callback so any diagnostic not located in the compilation's own syntax trees is silently dropped. It adds three metadata-reference tests and two docs notes.

requirementItems.text: Building a project that references a generic value type with `[MessagePackObject]` from another assembly completes without CS8785/AD0001.
The generated resolver for the consuming project is still produced in that situation.
The trigger matrix from the report is covered: generic + value type + referenced assembly crashes; non-generic structs and generic classes already work and must keep working.
Existing diagnostics for types declared in the compilation being analysed keep their current locations and keep being reported.
No behaviour change for types declared in source (regression tests must still pass).
The fix is in the analyzer/generator (`MessagePack.SourceGenerator`), not a workaround in user code.
The change is small and reviewable; no unrelated dependency or build changes.

claims.statement: The BothStringAndIntKeyAreNull diagnostic no longer indexes DeclaringSyntaxReferences[0]; it uses GetPropertyIdentifierLocation, which returns null for metadata properties instead of throwing IndexOutOfRangeException.
The MemberNeedsKey diagnostic now uses DeclaringSyntaxReferences.FirstOrDefault()?.GetSyntax().GetLocation(), so a metadata member yields a null location instead of throwing.

With these fixes, a [MessagePackObject] class with a member of closed generic struct type from a referenced assembly (including a record struct) builds with no CS8785/AD0001 and still emits the resolver (e.g. TempProject.MyResolver.g.cs).

Every analyzer diagnostic reported through TypeCollector's reportDiagnostic callback is now filtered. It is forwarded only if its location is in source and its syntax tree belongs to the current compilation. All other diagnostics are dropped silently.

The global diagnostic filter is a broader change than the crash fix needs. Diagnostics with Location.None or a location in a different compilation that were previously reported (e.g. null-location MemberNeedsKey, or diagnostics for in-source types located via other trees) are now suppressed.
Diagnostics for types and members declared in the compilation being analysed keep the same locations and are still reported, so existing analyzer tests pass unchanged.

The BothStringAndIntKeyAreNull location for source properties is unchanged. GetPropertyIdentifierLocation uses 'as PropertyDeclarationSyntax' where the old code used a hard cast, which returns null instead of throwing for a non-property declaration.

The new tests ClosedGenericStruct_FromMetadataReference, ClosedGenericRecordStruct_FromMetadataReference and ClosedGenericStruct_FromMetadataReference_UnkeyedMember each compile the defining source to a metadata-only image and fail on any analyzer/generator diagnostic. They also assert that the expected resolver hint name is generated.

The new tests cover the report's trigger matrix, including the non-crashing controls (non-generic struct and generic class from a referenced assembly). They cover only generic structs and a record struct.
The new tests fail on the pre-fix code (they reproduce the AD0001/CS8785 crash), and the UnkeyedMember test exercises the MemberNeedsKey path.

README.md adds a 'Generic types from referenced assemblies' section promising that closed generic types, including generic value types and record structs, from referenced assemblies work as members. It also says diagnostics about their members are reported by the defining assembly.

doc/analyzers/MsgPack004.md now states that the analyzer reports only on members declared in the project being compiled, and that unattributed members of referenced types are reported by the defining project. This generalises beyond MsgPack004 and beyond the changed paths, since the filter applies to all diagnostics.

Documentation additions and the new private helper methods (GetPropertyIdentifierLocation, ReportIfLocatedInCompilation) are not requested by any requirement item. No dependencies, build files or public API change.

verdicts.reasoning: The diff wraps the single reportDiagnostic delegate, so the filter applies to every diagnostic path. That is wider than the crash fix, which needed only the three DeclaringSyntaxReferences[0] sites replaced. Null-location diagnostics, and any diagnostic whose tree is not in this compilation, are now dropped. One part of the claim's wording is inaccurate. Diagnostics for in-source types located via other trees of the same compilation still pass, because ContainsSyntaxTree is true for them. Only trees from a different compilation, or no location at all, are suppressed. F4 and N1 appear to hold for source-declared types, since source locations are unchanged. The example of a null-location MemberNeedsKey is plausible only for metadata members. For metadata members the old code crashed on [0], so no diagnostic was ever reported there.

evidence.note: HEAD: the BothStringAndIntKeyAreNull call site now passes GetPropertyIdentifierLocation(item) as the location. Message arguments are unchanged.

HEAD: the helper uses FirstOrDefault()?.GetSyntax() as PropertyDeclarationSyntax, then ?.Identifier.GetLocation(). For a source property this is the same identifier location as before; for a missing or non-property declaration it returns null instead of throwing.

BASE: the old code was ((PropertyDeclarationSyntax)item.DeclaringSyntaxReferences[0].GetSyntax()).Identifier.GetLocation(). That throws on an empty collection (IndexOutOfRange) and a hard cast throws InvalidCastException on a non-property node.

HEAD: the reporter is now wrapped by ReportIfLocatedInCompilation (defined at line 1444). It drops diagnostics whose location is not in a source tree of this compilation. Source-declared properties still pass, so their reported location is unchanged.

verdicts.reasoning: For a property declared in source, the declaration is a PropertyDeclarationSyntax. The new `as` cast and the old hard cast therefore both yield the same Identifier.GetLocation(), and the diagnostic descriptor and message arguments are identical. The code at line 888 handles indexers with `item.IsIndexer`; I did not read what it does, so I cannot rule out an indexer reaching line 985. The new wrapper can only suppress diagnostics located outside the compilation, which the base code would have crashed on, so it does not alter source locations. verdicts.basis: Direct code reading of the three tests, the shared helper and the test verifier base class. No execution, so I did not confirm the tests pass.

evidence.note: The three tests each call RunWithMetadataReferenceAsync with their own define/usage source and expected hint name: TempProject.MyResolver.g.cs, App.AppResolver.g.cs, TempProject.MyResolver.g.cs.

The helper compiles the defining source with Emit into a MemoryStream and loads it with MetadataReference.CreateFromImage, so the consumer sees no syntax. It then runs VerifyCS.Test with no ExpectedDiagnostics, so any diagnostic fails the run. It then runs the generator driver, asserts no warning-or-worse diagnostics, and asserts the hint-name list contains the expected resolver name.
The Test sets CompilerDiagnostics.Warnings and runs every DiagnosticAnalyzer in the analyzer assembly plus the generator. CS8785 and AD0001 are warnings, so they would fail the run.
The resolver file name is the namespace-qualified resolver name plus .g.cs, which matches the hint names the tests assert.

verdicts.reasoning: Each test meets both parts of the claim. The first run, through the analyzer/generator test harness, fails on any diagnostic. The second run drives the generator directly and asserts the resolver hint name is present. The defining assembly is a compiled image referenced as metadata, so no syntax is available to the consumer. Two details do not weaken the claim. First, the first run uses SkipGeneratedSourcesCheck, so the hint-name assertion comes only from the separate driver run. Second, the image is a full in-memory assembly, not a reference assembly. I did not verify that the tests fail on BASE.

The three tests compile the defining assembly to an image and reference it as metadata. They run the verifier with no expected diagnostics, then assert the resolver hint name is generated. They contain no field members, so any failure on base would come from compiler-generated backing fields.

The reportDiagnostic callback is wrapped in ReportIfLocatedInCompilation.

ReportIfLocatedInCompilation drops diagnostics whose location is not in a syntax tree of the current compilation. Its remarks say that problems in metadata types are reported by the compilation that defines them.

verdicts.reasoning: BASE crashed because it indexed DeclaringSyntaxReferences[0] at TypeCollector.cs:985 and :1077, and metadata symbols have no syntax references. HEAD makes both accesses null-safe and drops any diagnostic that has no location in the current compilation. So the consuming project no longer reports problems in members of a referenced type. This matches the README sentence that diagnostics are reported by the defining assembly rather than the consumer. The wording is slightly loose. The consumer drops these diagnostics, and the defining assembly reports them only if the analyzer runs there. I read the whole path only for the diagnostic side. The promise that closed generic value types and record structs work as members rests on the removed indexers. I did not trace that to the generated code or to a test.

verdicts.basis: Direct code reading of the diagnostic filter and both MsgPack004 report paths in TypeCollector.cs. Nothing was executed and no test was read.

evidence.note: The doc says the analyzer reports only on members declared in the compiled project. It also says an unattributed public member of a referenced type must be fixed in its defining project.
All analyzer diagnostics go through ReportIfLocatedInCompilation, so the filter does apply to every diagnostic, not just MsgPack004. This supports the generalisation part of the claim.
The filter keeps a diagnostic only if its location is in source and in a syntax tree of this compilation. It judges the diagnostic's location, not whether the member was declared in the project.

When a source type inherits unattributed public members from a base type in a referenced assembly, MsgPack004 (BaseTypeContainsUnattributedPublicMembers) is reported at the base-type clause in the consuming project. The filter lets it through because that location is in source. The same pattern appears at lines 1087-1095.
BaseTypeContainsUnattributedPublicMembers uses the MsgPack004 ID (AttributeMessagePackObjectMembersId), so this case falls under the doc page.

verdicts.reasoning: The doc text exists and is accurate for members declared directly on a metadata type. Those diagnostics have no source location, so the filter drops them. The filter also covers all diagnostics, as the claim says. The doc statement is too absolute, though. When a source type derives from a referenced base type with unattributed public members, MsgPack004 is still reported in the consuming project, at the base-type reference. That contradicts "only reports on members declared in the project" and "must be fixed in its defining project". The consumer can fix it locally, for example by changing the base type or ignoring the member. I did not check whether the defining project actually runs the analyzer. I also did not verify how the doc's wording was chosen against F4.
verdicts.humanQuestion: Should the doc mention that inherited unattributed members from a referenced base type are still reported as MsgPack004 at the base-type clause in the consuming project? If not, is the absolute wording intended?
